gloss: A glass or plastic door that closes off a shower.

gloss: A small dish that holds a bar of soap.

gloss: A small wooden toilet building standing outside, with no plumbing.

The old farm still had two *outhouses*.

gloss: A small toilet or bowl that a young child learns to use.

Once *enamel* is gone, it doesn't grow back.
The dentist said my *enamel* is thin.

gloss: An unpleasant smell coming from someone's mouth.
examples: Coffee gives him *bad breath*.
Mouthwash only hides *bad breath*.
*Bad breath* can be a sign of gum trouble.

gloss: A small pointed stick for getting food out from between the teeth.
examples: He was chewing on a *toothpick*.
There's a jar of *toothpicks* by the register.
Use a *toothpick*, not your fingernail.

gloss: A plastic and wire device worn to keep teeth straight after braces.
examples: Wear your *retainer* every night.
He lost his *retainer* in the cafeteria.
*Retainers* cost a few hundred dollars to replace.

gloss: A removable set of false teeth.
examples: Grandpa soaks his *dentures* overnight.
Her *dentures* fit better after the adjustment.
He got *dentures* at seventy.
contrast: Normally plural: a set of *dentures*, not a denture.

gloss: Treatment that makes teeth look whiter.
examples: She paid for professional *whitening*.
*Whitening* can make your teeth sensitive.
The strips promise *whitening* in two weeks.

gloss: Infection of the gums that can loosen the teeth.
examples: Flossing helps prevent *gum disease*.
*Gum disease* is more common than people think.
He's being treated for early *gum disease*.

gloss: The slow breaking down of a tooth that produces cavities.
examples: Sugar is the main cause of *tooth decay*.
Fluoride slows *tooth decay*.
The X-ray showed *tooth decay* between two molars.

gloss: A pain in a tooth.
examples: I've had a *toothache* since Sunday.
A bad *toothache* kept him up all night.
*Toothaches* rarely go away on their own.
contrast: The -ache ending is pronounced AYK, as in cake.

gloss: One of the four back teeth that come in during your late teens or twenties.
examples: My *wisdom tooth* is coming in sideways.
She had all four *wisdom teeth* pulled.
Not everyone gets *wisdom teeth*.
contrast: Irregular plural: one *wisdom tooth*, two wisdom teeth.

gloss: One of the first small teeth that a child loses around age six.
examples: He lost his first *baby tooth* today.
All her *baby teeth* are gone now.
A *baby tooth* usually falls out on its own.
contrast: Americans say *baby tooth*; the British often say milk tooth. The plural is baby teeth.

gloss: Dental treatment that cleans out the inside of a damaged tooth.
examples: He needs a *root canal* on his back molar.
The *root canal* took two visits.
*Root canals* aren't as painful as people say.

gloss: A dentist who straightens crooked teeth with braces.
examples: The *orthodontist* tightened her braces.
We see the *orthodontist* every six weeks.
Most *orthodontists* start treatment around age twelve.

gloss: One of the flat front teeth used for biting.
examples: He chipped an *incisor* on a fork.
Your top *incisors* do most of the biting.
The dentist filled a small cavity in an *incisor*.

gloss: Small white flakes of dead skin that fall from the scalp.
examples: This shampoo is supposed to stop *dandruff*.
He brushed the *dandruff* off his collar.
Dry winter air makes *dandruff* worse.

gloss: A skin condition that produces pimples, mostly on the face.
examples: Teenagers often struggle with *acne*.
The dermatologist gave her a cream for *acne*.
Scrubbing too hard can make *acne* worse.

gloss: A small raised red spot on the skin.
examples: He woke up with a *pimple* on his chin.
Don't pick at *pimples*.
A *pimple* usually clears up in a few days.

gloss: A tiny dark plug of oil in a pore of the skin.
examples: She has *blackheads* on her nose.
The strip is supposed to pull out *blackheads*.
One *blackhead* isn't worth worrying about.

gloss: The unpleasant smell of stale sweat.
examples: Deodorant keeps *body odor* under control.
The gym reeked of *body odor*.
Nobody wants to be told they have *body odor*.

gloss: Sweat, or the process of sweating.
examples: *Perspiration* ran down his forehead.
The shirt was soaked with *perspiration*.
*Perspiration* is how the body cools itself.
contrast: *Perspiration* is the polite word; in ordinary speech Americans say sweat.

gloss: The egg of a head louse, stuck to a hair.
examples: The school nurse checked the kids for *nits*.
Every *nit* has to be combed out.
*Nits* look like tiny white specks.

gloss: Red, sore skin caused by shaving.
examples: He got *razor burn* on his neck.
Shaving cream helps prevent *razor burn*.
*Razor burn* usually fades in a day.

gloss: A hair that curls back and grows into the skin.
examples: He gets *ingrown hairs* after shaving.
An *ingrown hair* can look like a pimple.
Exfoliating helps with *ingrown hairs*.

gloss: A patch of thick hard skin, usually on a hand or foot.
examples: He has *calluses* from playing guitar.
A pumice stone smooths a *callus* down.
Her heels were covered in *calluses*.
contrast: The noun is *callus*; callous, spelled with an o, is the adjective meaning unfeeling.

gloss: The strip of skin at the base of a fingernail.
examples: Push your *cuticles* back gently.
Don't cut your *cuticles*; it invites infection.
The *cuticle* around that nail is torn.

gloss: The soft yellow substance that forms inside the ear.
examples: *Earwax* actually protects the ear canal.
The doctor flushed out a plug of *earwax*.
Cotton swabs push *earwax* in deeper.

gloss: An itchy fungal infection of the skin between the toes.
examples: He picked up *athlete's foot* at the pool.
*Athlete's foot* spreads in damp locker rooms.
The cream cleared up his *athlete's foot* in a week.
